_meta.rule: One row per retired, parked, or adopted pattern. A row without a shape, a sample, a regime, a verdict, a killing fact and its date, or an anchor is a tombstone with no body; it is named as such and never filled in. This file is the machine copy; docs/lore/ARCHIVE.md is the reader's copy; scripts/check-patterns refuses a drift between them.

verdicts.RETIRED: The record refused it: a counted failure, a dominating sibling, or a verdict the archive can quote.
verdicts.PARKED: A dated, living candidate the record cannot yet seat. No number; a review date; a place in the forward lane.
verdicts.ADOPTED: Other people's failure, kept so no session repeats it under a new name.

entries.name: the unseated memory
entries.shape: A room that ships its seats before it ships the memory of what the seats paid for.
entries.sample: The whole pack through v1.17.0: eight seats, forty-eight agent files, a counted record, and zero archive entries. The archive was named in four surfaces and held in none.
entries.regime: The seven-seat and whole-house eras, v1.0.0 to v1.17.0.
entries.killing: The registry lands with this file and scripts/check-patterns refuses a row without a sample; the archive page is the reader's copy of the same rows. A retirement that cannot name its sample now fails the gate.

entries.name: the role-split agent files
entries.shape: One seat, three files per host: the seat, the review, and the build as separate agents.
entries.sample: The claude host carried twenty-one agent files before the merge and seven after it; six dialects carried forty-eight files at the whole-house release, one per seat.
entries.regime: The multi-file agent era, v1.0.0 to v1.8.0.
entries.killing: One file per seat, the role picked from the brief: twenty-one files became seven on the claude host at commit b6c31ff (v1.9.0), then eight when the machine seat landed.

entries.name: the hand-copied lore pages
entries.shape: A release surface whose pages are copied by hand from another tree and cannot be re-derived from their own sources.
entries.sample: Five static lore pages at v1.1.0 (canon, board, scenes, pre-history, gallery); zero after the site trim at commit 9e6d4da, and zero generated pages until this era.
entries.regime: The static-mirror era, v1.1.0 to v1.3.0.
entries.killing: The trim removed the copied pages (commit 9e6d4da). This era renders every lore page from the pack's own sources, and a page that cannot name its source hash fails its freshness check.

entries.name: the self-counted literal
entries.shape: A count that names itself instead of deriving itself: the board's seat total written as a constant inside the check.
entries.sample: At v1.17.0 the board check printed the length of its own seat tuple, eight, while the board file held eight sections. The literal agreed with the tree and measured nothing; a ninth section would have passed.
entries.killing: The count derives from the board's own sections (commit for this era, scripts/check-board line 106): a board that drops a seat or grows one now fails closed.

entries.name: the unbacked scene number
entries.shape: A format model that cites a denominator no file holds, and keeps the room's trust by sounding like a sample.
entries.sample: The scene book at v1.17.0 cited one hundred fourteen occurrences across four surfaces and two qualifying packages. The tree held zero archive entries and zero packages, so the number was a hymn with a stage.
entries.regime: The scene book before the registry.
entries.killing: Every scene citation resolves to a registry id or the number is cut; scripts/check-patterns fails a citation with no row, and the machine scene now cites P-002's counted sample.

entries.name: Knight Capital
entries.shape: A deploy that runs an untested path on live state: the release is the failure surface.
entries.sample: August 1, 2012: a deploy left a legacy flag armed, the machines woke the old code, and for forty-five minutes orders nobody had sized went out. Roughly four hundred forty million dollars was gone by the close, and the firm was sold by morning.
entries.killing: Failure: the deploy is a failure surface. Speed: forty-five minutes. Takes: the firm's capital and its independence.

entries.name: Ariane 5
entries.shape: Code reused outside the envelope it was tested in: the number fit in the old body and not in the new one.
entries.sample: June 4, 1996: flight software inherited from Ariane 4 converted a horizontal velocity that fit in sixty-four bits into a sixteen-bit value. The conversion overflowed, both inertial units failed, and the launcher broke up about forty seconds into flight with its payload.
entries.killing: Failure: inherited code in a new body. Speed: forty seconds. Takes: the rocket, the payload, and the assumption that a reused line is a tested line.

entries.name: Therac-25
entries.shape: A race condition the interface hides: the machine reports a fault while doing the harm.
entries.sample: 1985 to 1987: a radiotherapy machine's control software raced its operator's keystrokes; the display reported a malfunction while the dose went out. Patients were injured and killed while the screen said the run had stopped.
entries.killing: Failure: the display was trusted over the state. Speed: one keystroke. Takes: the patient, and the assumption that a green screen means safe.

entries.name: Challenger
entries.shape: A known failure mode reclassified as acceptable under schedule pressure: the normalization of deviance.
entries.sample: January 28, 1986: engineers had watched the solid rocket joints erode across earlier flights and had been argued into treating the erosion as normal. The launch was called on a cold morning; the joint failed seventy-three seconds in.
entries.killing: Failure: a known defect renamed as a margin. Speed: seventy-three seconds. Takes: the crew, and the institution's habit of hearing its own reassurance.

entries.name: Denver
entries.shape: An integration grown past the point any test can describe it: the system is a diagram of intentions, not a body.
entries.sample: 1994 to 1995: the airport's automated baggage system was commissioned as one enormous integration with no stage that could fail small. It missed the airport's opening, ran months late, and was partly dismantled after costing far more than its plan.
entries.killing: Failure: integration without a seam. Speed: months. Takes: the opening, the budget, and the project's credibility.

entries.name: Healthcare.gov
entries.shape: A launch under load with no load test that could fail: the first hour is the test.
entries.sample: October 1, 2013: the federal marketplace opened to national traffic with no end-to-end load test that could have refused the launch. A small fraction of visitors completed an application in the first weeks; the repair took months.
entries.killing: Failure: the load test was a promise, not a gate. Speed: the first hour. Takes: public trust and a year of the program.

entries.name: LTCM
entries.shape: Certainty fails whole: a model that assumes correlation and liquidity, levered until the assumption is the position.
entries.sample: 1998: a fund of prize-winning models was levered roughly twenty-five times into convergence trades. Russia defaulted, credit ran, spreads widened, and about four point six billion dollars of equity went in under four months. Fourteen banks rescued the book because its failure would have been theirs.
entries.killing: Failure: a book that cannot be wrong until it is. Speed: weeks. Takes: the fund, its lenders, and the belief that the past is a forecast.

entries.name: The August 2007 quake
entries.shape: Diversification among cousins is not diversification: many names, one trade.
entries.sample: August 2007: quantitative funds that had never traded together lost together in one week. Similar signals, similar positions, similar lenders. One delevered, sold what the others held, the marks moved, and the next margin call forced the next seller.
entries.killing: Failure: a crowd of similar mechanisms is one position wearing several names. Speed: days. Takes: the cousins, and the word diversification as comfort.

entries.name: The Flash Crash
entries.shape: The exit was never there when the print was: liquidity is a verb, and it leaves before the price does.
entries.sample: May 6, 2010: one large seller moved about four point one billion dollars of S&P 500 futures in twenty minutes into a book already leaving. Liquidity passed the same contracts back and forth, then withdrew; some issues printed at a penny. The tape recovered in minutes; the assumption did not.
entries.killing: Failure: a market-order chain is not an exit plan. Speed: minutes. Takes: the belief that intraday liquidity is a noun.

entries.name: Volmageddon
entries.shape: The protection that ruins its holders: the hedge is the position.
entries.sample: February 5, 2018: a product sold insurance on volatility while the market stayed calm. When the market moved, the note's own rebalancing demanded the futures it was short, and the spike fed the unwind; the note terminated down about ninety-six percent on the day it was held as protection.
entries.killing: Failure: the hedge that ruins its holders is not a hedge. Speed: one session. Takes: the holders, the issuers' reputations, and the word hedge as comfort.

entries.name: Sarao
entries.shape: The myth that hides the structure is the second failure: the story of one actor covers the market design that let the act work.
entries.sample: 2010 to 2015: a single trader's spoofing orders were presented as the explanation for a market's behavior. The orders were real; the structure that made them profitable, and the field that read them as intent, were the larger fact. The villain was easier to publish than the design.
entries.killing: Failure: the myth is the second failure. Speed: years. Takes: the truth, and everyone who preferred the villain.
